acceptedAnswer.text: Framing in photography means choosing what appears within the image boundaries, what is left out and how the included elements relate. Your viewpoint, timing and choice of edges influence what the photograph communicates. A frame within a frame is one technique within this wider craft.

mainEntity.name: How is framing different from composition?

acceptedAnswer.text: Composition concerns the arrangement and relationships of elements throughout a photograph. Framing focuses on the boundaries and viewpoint that determine what is included, excluded or cut through. They overlap: changing the frame changes the composition.

mainEntity.name: What are examples of framing in photography?

acceptedAnswer.text: Examples include moving closer to exclude a distraction, leaving space around a person to show their surroundings, changing position to separate overlapping shapes, or photographing through a doorway. Each choice changes the context, emphasis or relationships within the image.

mainEntity.name: When should you use a frame within a frame?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use a doorway, window, arch or foliage when it adds useful depth, context or emphasis. Compare a version with the surrounding frame and one without it. Keep the version that best supports what you want to communicate; the technique is optional.

mainEntity.name: How can beginners improve their framing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Begin by noticing what interests you, then try different viewpoints and boundaries. When time allows, check all four edges for unintended distractions or overlaps. Compare two versions afterwards and explain how the framing changed the feeling or meaning.

mainEntity.name: Does every photograph need one clear subject?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A photograph can centre on one subject or explore a relationship, mood, pattern or space. Making a subject clear is a useful exercise, but ambiguity and several areas of interest can also contribute. Judge the framing by what the image communicates.

mainEntity.name: Does good framing always need balance and clean edges?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Balance and uncluttered edges can help, but deliberate imbalance, cropped elements or complexity may express tension, movement or context. The useful habit is noticing their effect and deciding whether it serves the photograph.
